scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent English A1 asteroid comprehension assessment awaiting external pedagogical validation.

questions.q: Why is an asteroid different from a star?
choices: It is always bigger than Earth.
It does not make its own light.
It can only be seen in the morning.
It moves without going around the Sun.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one says stars give light, but asteroids do not produce their own light.

questions.q: What can we understand about the size of asteroids?
choices: They all have the same size.
They are smaller than every car.
Each one is as big as a mountain.
Some are much larger than others.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one compares very small asteroids with others bigger than mountains.

questions.q: Why do scientists take pictures of asteroids more than once?
choices: To change the rocks' colours.
To make asteroids move faster.
To follow where the rocks travel.
To measure how many stars there are.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains that scientists watch the movement of asteroids.

questions.q: What helps scientists see a distant asteroid?
choices: A large telescope pointed into the sky.
A small clock near their computer.
A map of the nearest museum.
A photograph of a mountain.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes telescopes as tools for seeing things far away.

questions.q: Why is the shape of Ceres special compared with most asteroids?
choices: It has no place in the solar system.
It looks exactly like a car.
It is round while many are irregular.
It gives out light like a star.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Ceres is round, but most asteroids are not.

questions.q: What makes a museum meteorite interesting?
choices: It is an ancient piece of rock from space.
It was made by people in a factory.
It is a small moon around Ceres.
It is always lighter than water.
questions.explanation: The museum example describes an old piece of space rock called a meteorite.

questions.q: Why do scientists keep watching objects in space?
choices: Because all big impacts happen every day.
Because learning about them can help protect people.
Because all pieces of rock reach the ground.
Because the Sun moves around each asteroid.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph connects watching the sky with learning and safety.

questions.q: A small space rock enters the air around Earth. What may happen?
choices: It immediately becomes a planet.
It grows as big as a mountain.
It starts making its own light forever.
It burns up before it reaches the ground.
questions.explanation: Many small pieces burn up in the atmosphere, according to the last paragraph.

questions.q: Your friend thinks an asteroid is a star. What is the best correction?
choices: Every asteroid is the same size as a star.
An asteroid is a rock that moves around the Sun.
Asteroids are made only of bright light.
Asteroids never move through space.
questions.explanation: An asteroid is described as a space rock following an orbit around the Sun.

questions.q: What could you do to learn about a new asteroid?
choices: Guess its orbit from a single word.
Wait for the asteroid to visit your school.
Use only a map of Earth's oceans.
Observe where it goes with a telescope.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph shows how repeated observations help scientists follow an asteroid.
